newsitem.title: GERMANY: Frankfurt can be top euro centre - Deutsche's Breuer.
newsitem.headline: Frankfurt can be top euro centre - Deutsche's Breuer.

text.p: Long experience as home to Europe's anchor currency gives Frankfurt a strong chance to become the top centre for the euro under monetary union, Deutsche Bank AG's future chief Rolf Breuer said.

"We are the deutschemark financial centre. We have a major chance to also become the euro financial centre. This is an unique opportunity and I hope we use it," Breuer said in a speech to a banking audience late on Wednesday.

But Breuer, a well-established champion of German financial market developments, also said that the euro was not only Frankfurt's best chance of holding its own against giants like London, Tokyo or New York -- it might be its only one.

Once European economic and monetary union (EMU) robs Frankfurt of its one major draw -- the mark -- the city's many disadvantages in terms of restrictive labour policies and lack of trained personnel will become even more evident, he said.

"We need to catch up. If the LSE (London School of Economics) or Harvard wants to discuss development of new products or something similar, then Germany is not its choice. And one of the reasons to locate in a financial centre is the existence of an intellectual basis for what heppens there."

Breuer praised German legislators for co-operating in reforms over the past years to promote efficiency on German markets, but said the message that conditions had changed had not filtered through to a broader public.
Europe suffered in any case from an "embarrassment" of stock exchanges, which would become obsolete in an increasingly globalised world.

The real competition for the future would not come from places physically home to a stock exchange but from "virtual exchanges" formed from electronic links between markets worldwide using increasingly advanced technologies.
Noting that over half the participants on Germany's DTB futures and options exchange were not German, Breuer said that remote participation in a market "is not a transient thing, it is a trend."
That, he said, made it essential for financial centres to focus on electronic platforms for trading rather than the trading floor, which could not facilitate remote membership.

Germany is already well on the way to accomplishing a move to full electronic trading, which is to be introduced in phases and should be almost fully functional by the planned euro launch date in January 1999.
On the chances that the Frankfurt bourse trading floor will survive this upheaval, Breuer merely said: "I already know who the winner will be."
